item.title: U.S. Federal Reserve keeps rates unchanged despite elevated inflation, gives little signal of its next move
item.description: The U.S. Federal Reserve kept its key rate unchanged Wednesday at about 3.9% despite elevated inflation, while providing little hint about the central bank’s next moves.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Federal Reserve kept its key rate unchanged Wednesday at about 3.9% despite elevated inflation, while providing little hint about the central bank’s next moves. “Inflation remains elevated,” the Fed said in a statement released after its two-day policy meeting. Holding off on an increase will allow “the accumulation of more information” that will help determine what policy the Fed should pursue “to ensure a timely return of inflation” to the central bank’s two per cent inflation target, the statement said. The Fed, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, raised its benchmark rate last month for the first time in three years, defying U.S. President Donald Trump’s demands for rate cuts, in an effort to get inflation back to its two per cent target in a “timelier” manner. The Fed is tasked by Congress to combat inflation, and it does so by lifting rates to slow borrowing and spending and cool price increases. Two Fed officials dissented from Wednesday’s decision, with Fed governor Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack voting in favor of hiking rates by a quarter point. Cook has been targeted by the Trump administration, which tried to fire her last year, though the Supreme Court in June ruled she could keep her job while litigation played out. No president has fired a Fed governor before, a sign of the Fed’s longstanding independence from day-to-day politics. Trump renewed his attempt to remove Cook last month by setting up a committee to look into allegations Cook committed mortgage fraud, which she has denied. Christopher Rugaber, The Associated Press

item.title: Wealthsimple raises $425M in latest equity round, putting its valuation at $13.8B
item.description: Wealthsimple Inc. says it has raised $425 million in financing from its existing investors, which it says will help it expand its services.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Wealthsimple Inc. says it has raised $425 million in financing from its existing investors, which it says will help it expand its services and challenge incumbent lenders. The company announced in a news release Tuesday that the equity round, which includes a $300 million primary offering and a $125 million secondary offering, will put its valuation at $13.8 billion. The company says the secondary offering will give employees an opportunity to “share in the value they’ve helped create.” GIC, the Singapore sovereign wealth fund, led the round of financing along with participation from Power Corp. of Canada, IGM Financial Inc., the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and others. Michael Katchen, Wealthsimple’s CEO and co-founder, says the group of investors know the business well, and the support will help it continue to innovate. Wealthsimple says it plans to use the money to help grow its business, including personal banking as well as trading and investment products. --- Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

item.title: ‘We think it’s premature’: Expert reaction to the Bank of Canada’s first rate hike since 2023
item.description: The Bank of Canada raised its key interest rate for the first time in more than three years on Wednesday, drawing mixed reaction from experts and lawmakers.
item.dc:creator: Jordan Fleguel
item.content:encoded: The Bank of Canada raised its key interest rate for the first time in more than three years on Wednesday, drawing mixed reaction from experts and lawmakers. The central bank’s governor, Tiff Macklem, said in remarks Wednesday that elevated global energy prices could soon seep into other parts of the Canadian economy, and the hike was needed to reduce that risk. Earl Davis, head of fixed income and money markets at BMO Global Asset Management, told BNN Bloomberg following the bank’s decision that Macklem’s comments suggest the bank is “trying to get ahead of the game.” But a rate hike on its own won’t prevent the knock-on effects of higher oil prices, Davis said. “That will happen no matter what, but it prevents people from buying ahead of time and controlling inflation,” he said. “So (Macklem) is trying to get ahead of it, and that seems to be explicitly stated in the statement.” The bank’s decision to hike comes as Canada’s economy continues to grapple with uncertainty due to shifting geopolitical dynamics and a trading relationship with the U.S. that has fundamentally changed. Canadian workers have paid the price for the country’s economic sluggishness. Statistics Canada said earlier this month that the economy shed a net 68,300 jobs in September, effectively erasing the employment gains made earlier this year. ‘Pre-emptive hike’ Davis said that according to the Bank of Canada’s October Monetary Policy Report, released Wednesday, the bank has put a renewed emphasis on mitigating the impacts of a “persistent supply shock” in energy markets. “In layman’s terms, the persistence of how high oil has been, and the price of oil at this level for so long… will impact inflation expectations of consumers for the next six months to a year, which means they will buy more and consume more now to get ahead of inflation,” he said. “So, we see this hike as a pre-emptive hike.” Davis said the decision didn’t come as a surprise to him, as the 25-basis-point increase was widely expected, but he added that the move was likely made too early. “Why we think it’s premature is… last week we had a lot of equity volatility, a lot of risk of market nervousness, which has calmed down this week, but we expect that volatility to return and remain there for the fourth quarter, which adds to uncertainty,” he explained. RSM Canada economist Tu Nguyen said in an emailed statement to BNN Bloomberg that the bank’s “decidedly hawkish” tone sends a clear message. “This is the first hike in a hiking cycle. Expect the next rate hike as early as December – with more to follow in 2027,” she said. “The Bank of Canada won’t be alone in raising rates. Rather, it’s set to be one of several major central banks embarking on a hiking cycle… ahead of tightening global financial conditions in 2027 that could thwart growth.” ‘Silver lining’ Wednesday’s rate hike also comes at a time when many Canadians are struggling with the overall cost of living, and higher interest rates will be an additional challenge, said Ontario Premier Doug Ford in a post to X on Wednesday. “Higher rates won’t get oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz or lower tariffs on Canadian businesses,” he wrote. “They will only make life more expensive for Canadian families and workers, punishing them for something they can’t control.” Davis said that while the Bank of Canada may have moved into a hiking cycle too early, the decision may ultimately have “a silver lining.” “It may very well be the right thing in hindsight, but because it’s premature, the market was, prior to this, discounting an additional 100-basis-points-plus of hikes, including today’s,” he said. “We think that will be reduced now to possibly 75, or the market thinking the Bank of Canada will hike less over the coming year because today was a bit premature.” With files from CP24’s Phil Tsekouras and The Canadian Press

item.content:encoded:
Ernest Wong, Head of Research, Baskin Wealth Management Focus: North American Large Caps

Top Picks: Netflix , FirstService , Berkshire Hathaway MARKET OUTLOOK: Difficult stock market to navigate this year due to record concentration in artificial intelligence (AI) and very poor market breadth. Seeing impact of higher interest rates in the U.S. on data centres and housing. Consumer has remained resilient however. In Canada, the economy is still sluggish from tariff uncertainty and lower immigration levels and higher interest rates will hurt. Finding good opportunities in non-AI and energy related stocks at attractive valuations. How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google Market-moving news, fast:  Get the BNN Bloomberg App now Sign up for the Market Call Top Picks newsletter at  bnnbloomberg.ca/newsletters TOP PICKS: Ernest Wong's Top Picks: Netflix, FirstService & Berkshire Hathaway Ernest Wong, head of research at Baskin Wealth Management, shares his top stock picks to watch in the market.

Netflix (NFLX NASD) Stock down over 40 per cent over last year, facing disruption narrative amidst weak engagement in the U.S. Still believe in the business model: it is the largest streamer with most subscribers and profits, it can pivot to other types of content. Also gaining market share in international markets. Recently made management changes to improve content quality. Also has opportunities in sports and channels. Valuation extremely cheap at 15 times earnings, it will still grow double digits next year. FirstService (FSV TSX) Has two divisions: Property Management division and Brands business that does home renovations, property restoration, commercial roofing. Historically has been a great compounder with a good track record of entering new markets, building up strong brands, and gaining market share over independents. Stock has been weak due to weak housing market and lack of storms. Results appear to have bottomed as of last quarter. Stock trading at about 21 times earnings and management is buying back stock. Berkshire Hathaway (BRK.B NYSE) Has been concerns about Buffett’s retirement, but Greg Abel has been active with capital deployment: acquired Taylor Morrison and made a large Google investment. Will benefit from higher interest rates due to large cash position. Expect to have attractive investment opportunities as provider of liquidity. Stock trading at 1.5 times book value, has been repurchasing stock.
